subject: Support for Wasatch Community Gardens' CDBG Funding Request
comment: Dear Salt Lake City Council, My name is Miranda, and I'm your constituent living in the Avenues. I'm writing to request your support for Wasatch Community Gardens' (WCG's) application for $40,000 in CDBG funds to support its farm-based Green Team Job Training Program for women facing or experiencing homelessness. This program provides paid employment, job training, and mentorship at WCG's new City Farm on 1300 South, helping participants secure stable housing and jobs. Green Team members are challenged to learn, grow, and rediscover their strengths, even as they navigate difficult circumstances. A key part of the program's success is WCG's onsite Case Manager, who maintains a realistic caseload to support Green Team members while also assisting overworked shelter and outreach case managers. Over 100 Green Team graduates have transitioned to independent living, with 80% securing housing and employment within six months. The impact of this program extends far beyond individual participants. Green Team members play a critical role in ensuring thousands of individuals and families have access to fresh, nutritious food. All produce grown at City Farm is donated to low-income community members through WCG's partner organizations, distributing $100,000 worth of healthy food annually. In any given year, more than 40% of the Utah population served in shelters has received food grown by the Green Team at WCG's farm. With 12% of Utahns experiencing food insecurity and grocery prices rising, sustainable, local food sources are more critical than ever. WCG is the only broad-scale, garden-to-mouth nonprofit in Salt Lake City, providing growing space, food education, and distribution to shelters and community partners. Without CDBG support, Salt Lake City compromises this vital resource that not only feeds our community but also helps women reclaim stability in their lives. Please prioritize WCG's Green Team Job Training Program for CDBG funding. Thank you, Miranda Signorelli

subject: Comment in favor of Wasatch Community Gardens 2025-2026 CDBG Request for $40,000
comment: This note is in support of the 2025-2026 CDBG (Community Development Block Grant) request by the Wasatch Community Gardens (WCG) in the amount of $40,000. I am a District 2 resident and a City resident of 47 years. The 2023 Annual Report of WCG attests to its wide impact in neighborhood revitalization within the City and the broad support from the community in the form of monetary or in-kind donations. I am one of the raised bed gardeners at one of 18 community gardens that service around 620+ plot gardeners in the City - a small component of one of WCG's many activities. My observation about the garden — this one along the 9-Line Trail — is that it provides a community focus and anti-crime effects in the area throughout May through November each year. It is an exemplar of anti—neighborhood deterioration activities that are at the core of the CDBG program. The garden serves as a community focus point — a public food tax and bets provide fresh food to 9-Line Trail users. Visits from external groups, such as surrounding schools and youth programs, introduce gardening to many residents. The constant outdoor presence of the gardeners deters criminal elements in the area. Our members constantly remove trash, including drug user injection needles, from along the 9-Line Trail near the garden, suppress graffiti, and work with or, where appropriate, request relocation of unsheltered camps. Our members have remained resilient in these efforts despite having the garden's tool shed broken into multiple times by criminal elements. I understand the CDBG request concerns another component of WCG's many community revitalization efforts — its employment training program for displaced and unsheltered women. I have occasionally seen this program and its participants at WCG's main garden production facility, the "Green Phoenix." It functions well. Women-directed gardening (or employment training has long been a component of the United States gardening movement. It goes back to its foundations in the World War I "Liberty" garden program by the War Department. WCG successfully continues that long tradition. That early WWI program, which was continued through the WWII Victory gardens, was key to providing about one-third of the nation's produce during and immediately after the two world wars. That contribution of produce during times of distress allowed the United States to redirect commercial agriculture from domestic production to international relief. The Liberty gardens allowed the United States to send its commercial agricultural output to feed Europe during the first two post-war years after each conflict. This seemingly under-related historical note underscores another key future need for the WCG programs. The country will being responding - on the local neighborhood level - to a likely deep recession caused by the current federal administration's intention to generate economic chaos as a political strategy. subject: Support for Wasatch Community Gardens' CDBG Funding Request
comment: Dear Salt Lake City Council, My name is Susan Masotti, and I'm your constituent living in the Avenues. I'm writing to request your support for Wasatch Community Gardens' (WCG's) application for $40,000 in CDBG funds to support its farm-based Green Team Job Training Program for women facing or experiencing homelessness. This program provides paid employment, job training, and mentorship at WCG's new City Farm on 1300 South, helping participants secure stable housing and jobs. Green Team members are challenged to learn, grow, and rediscover their strengths, even as they navigate difficult circumstances. A key part of the program's success is WCG's onsite Case Manager, who maintains a realistic caseload to support Green Team members while also assisting overworked shelter and outreach case managers. Over 100 Green Team graduates have transitioned to independent living, with 80% securing housing and employment within six months. The impact of this program extends far beyond individual participants. Green Team members play a critical role in ensuring thousands of individuals and families have access to fresh, nutritious food. All produce grown at City Farm is donated to low-income community members through WCG's partner organizations, distributing $100,000 worth of healthy food annually. In any given year, more than 40% of the Utah population served in shelters has received food grown by the Green Team at WCG's farm. With 12% of Utahns experiencing food insecurity and grocery prices rising, sustainable, local food sources are more critical than ever. WCG is the only broad-scale, garden-to-mouth nonprofit in Salt Lake City, providing growing space, food education, and distribution to shelters and community partners. Without CDBG support, Salt Lake City compromises this vital resource that not only feeds our community but also helps women reclaim stability in their lives. Please prioritize WCG's Green Team Job Training Program for CDBG funding. Thank you, Susan Masotti

subject: SLC City Park Security & Alternative Security Solution
comment: Dear Councilmen Puy and Wharton, and CAO Love, I'm writing as a constituent (homeowner in Central 9th) in regard to the Salt Lake Tribune's 4/10 article addressing additional security measures to be taken in our city parks. I'm also writing to introduce you to a potential alternative solution to security guards. I'm on the Board of Directors of an SLC-based remote video monitoring company called Blue Eye (think virtual security guards). Blue Eye's advanced AI analyzes video camera feeds to detect suspicious behavior, escalating to a human operator who then leverages speakers hosted on-premises to address the suspect(s) with personalized messaging i.e. "To the man in the black hoodie, this park is closed and you are trespassing. Please leave immediately or SLPD will be dispatched". Assuming the individual(s) remain undeterred, Blue Eye will then manage the dispatch of police to the property and stay engaged until the situation is resolved. Further, behind the scenes we capture robust data on site-level activity in our customer accessible Reporting Portal, which could help inform future security and policing strategies. Since cost is understandably an issue, I wanted to note that Blue Eye's service is approximately one-fifth the price of physical security guards, despite the fact that guards lack visibility, cannot cover large surface areas, and are prone to human error. We could also explore meaningful volume discounts as we're keen to support our hometown (and, selfishly, want our parks safe too!). Recognizing that our city parks may not currently have video surveillance infrastructure in place, we also have a large network of camera manufacturers we work with and could assist you in sourcing that hardware (including solar power cameras that require no power source). The article is well-timed as there's been internal discussions at Blue Eye at how we can work more closely with SLPD to make our home city safer. Please let me know if you're interested in learning more, and I can connect you with representatives from our sales and engineering teams to provide a demo. As a father of a 3 month old, many thanks for taking important steps to keep our parks safe. Cheers, Sean Cushing -- Sean Cushing Managing Director, Bandon Holdings

subject: Request for Rezoning Consideration of Parcels to MU-8 in the Central Community
comment: Dear Members of the Salt Lake City Council, My name is Nate Leishman, and I am reaching out on behalf of Colmena Group regarding a request to rezone our parcels as part of Salt Lake City's zone consolidation amendment . Our parcels consisting of parcel # REDACTED totaling 1.54 acres located at approximately REDACTED, Salt Lake City, UT. After careful consideration, we would like to formally request that these parcels be considered for upzoning to the MU-8 (Mixed-Use, High-Density) designation. We believe that rezoning our properties to MU-8 is both appropriate and beneficial for several key reasons: 1. Alignment with the Central Community Master Plan: The MU-8 zone aligns with the city's goals for mixed-use development that promotes the integration of residential, commercial, and civic uses. Our parcels are located in an area designated for such development, and we believe that this zoning change would support the city's broader vision for growth and urban revitalization. 2. State Street enhancement o Encourage redevelopment along State Street o Increase height along state street o Neighborhood placemaking o Walkability 3. Encouraging Transit-Oriented Development (TOD): Our properties are well-positioned to support transit-oriented development, being near major transportation corridors and light rail stations. The MU-8 zoning would facilitate higher-density residential and commercial uses, helping to reduce automobile dependency and contribute to the city's goal of increasing walkability and transit access in urban areas. 4. Benefits to the City and Community: o Economic Growth: The MU-8 zone allows for diverse commercial activities alongside residential development. This can attract new businesses, create jobs, and provide more opportunities for local entrepreneurs. o Enhanced Housing Options: Upzoning to MU-8 will allow for the creation of additional housing units, contributing to the city's growing demand for both affordable and market-rate housing. o Community and Neighborhood Revitalization: By introducing higher-density, mixed-use developments, we can revitalize underutilized land, improve neighborhood aesthetics, and foster a vibrant community atmosphere. We are aware that obtaining the MU-8 zoning designation requires several steps to ensure that this change aligns with the community's needs and values. The steps we anticipate following include: 1. Review of the Master Plan and Zoning Compatibility: We will carefully review the Central Community Master Plan and the current zoning designations to ensure our proposal aligns with the city's goals. 2. Submission of Zoning Petition: A formal petition for rezoning will be submitted, detailing how the proposed development will adhere to the principles of mixed-use growth, transit-oriented development, and community enhancement. 3. Zoning Analysis and Evaluation: Our proposal will undergo an analysis to ensure it supports the city's vision for livable, sustainable, and integrated urban areas. 4. Community and Stakeholder Involvement: We are committed to engaging with the local community and stakeholders to address any concerns and ensure that the development aligns with their interests. 5. Planning and Zoning Commission Review: The proposal will be reviewed by the Planning and Zoning Commission, who will assess its compatibility with the city's broader development goals. 6. City Council Approval: Upon the Planning and Zoning Commission's recommendation, the final decision will be made by the City Council. We sincerely believe that rezoning our parcels to MU-8 will not only support the city's long-term growth strategy but will also bring meaningful benefits to the surrounding community. We are enthusiastic about the potential to contribute to Salt Lake City's development and would greatly appreciate your consideration of this request. Should you require any additional information or wish to discuss this proposal further, please do not hesitate to reach out. We look forward to working collaboratively with the City Council and the community to ensure the success of this project. Thank you for your time and consideration. Warm regards, NATE LEISHMAN

subject: What does or does not work...
comment: Wayne, I googled the rate of recidivism for Utah's jails and prisons and learned that the current rate is 46%, and the length of sentence seems to have little impact on recidivism. So, if what I am hearing is true, and we will be asking the Courts for longer mandated sentences, there is no evidence to suggest the added jail time will help more people. The only people longer sentences may help will be those charged with dealing with the homeless problem. If we can't see them, the problem is not a problem. The problem with that thinking is that when the mentally ill eventually leave jail, they will be struggling with the same issues. The number of people living on our streets will decline for a short period of time. The number of people in our jails will increase, but eventually they will leave jail and rejoin their ex-inmate friends on the street. And the bottom line is that if jail is the "solution", nothing may change. The only thing that will change is that we get to label a person an inmate instead of homeless. What will not change is the 46% needing help. They will still be a problem for both the homeless and criminal justice system. A seemingly endless and forever problem. We are developing a way of testing a theory. If jail does help an individual, we may be able to measure the impact jails have, or don't have, on a person and predict what will happen. We hope to be able to measure the impact all those "we can help you" programs (in and out of jail) have on a person. The more successful programs are, the lower the rate of recidivism. An added plus. If we can measure outcomes, taxpayers benefit. We can start directing funding to programs that help the most people. This is getting to be fun. We are working with some great people, Bernie

comment: To whom it may concern, Please Note: The acronym of SLC-PSP 2025 will be used throughout this email, the acronym refers to the Salt Lake City Public Safety Plan January 2025 produced by the Mayor of Salt Lake City (SLC) and her team. The occupants of the encampment can and have become hostile towards me taking photographs of their living conditions. Is it unreasonable to [...want the City to resolve quality of life issues like sanitation, discarded property, and illegal camping...] (SLC-PSP 2025, Pg. 11) for its citizens? Before anyone says, "there is no money for this", take one million dollars from the allotted m16.3 million dollar 2025 summer redesigning of Pioneer Park project. However, it is a money issue. Waiting 20-30 days for the HEART team (Homeless Engagement and Response Team) to arrive at each encampment and giving City service information to the same people over and over and overpromptly enables them and emboldens their brazen behavior to continue. subject: Petition PLNHLC2023-00571 Yalecrest - Upper Yale - Local Historic District
comment: Dear City Council Members, I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed inclusion of the 1800 to 1900 block of Yale Avenue to the local historic district. While I understand and appreciate the intention to preserve architectural heritage and cultural history, I believe this action would have several negative long-term consequences for current and future homeowners in the area. The historic designation imposes significant limitations on property owners' ability to make changes, updates, or rebuilds to their homes. This dramatically reduces flexibility for maintenance and necessary modernization, and can disincentivize much-needed investment in our properties. In many cases, these restrictions require materials or methods that are significantly more expensive, thus increasing the cost of ownership for residents who may already be financially stretched. Moreover, this designation could decrease property values—not increase them—by narrowing the pool of prospective buyers. Many potential homeowners are deterred by the red tape and high costs associated with historic guidelines, preferring homes that allow for flexibility with customization and updates. In addition, homes risk appearing tired or outdated over time due to limits on improvements, which may further hurt neighborhood vitality and overall curb appeal. It is important to preserve our city's history, but that must be balanced with the rights and needs of its residents. A forced inclusion into a historic district undermines surrounding homeowners' autonomy, equity, and ability to adapt to evolving standards of safety, sustainability, and livability. I urge the Council to reconsider this proposal and respect the voices of those who live in and care for these homes every day. Please do not impose restrictions that diminish the livability, value, and long-term sustainability of our community. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Todd Boren

subject: Objection to proposed zoning project 273 E 800 S
comment: To Whom It May Concern, I am writing to respectfully express my opposition to the proposed zoning change at 273 E 800 S to allow for a four-story, high-density housing development intended for individuals earning less than 30% of the Area Median Income (AMI), many of whom will require behavioral health support and 24/7 on-site services. While I fully support the need for compassionate and affordable housing across our city, I am concerned that this particular proposal places an undue burden on the central city—an area that has long carried more than its fair share of deeply affordable, service-based housing. It is time for other neighborhoods to step up and share in this critical responsibility. Furthermore, the success of vulnerable residents depends on their placement in safe, stable, and balanced communities. Our neighborhood already struggles with high crime rates, strained infrastructure, and limited access to essential services. According to Salt Lake City's own crime data, central city neighborhoods experience some of the highest rates of property and violent crime in the city. Adding another high-needs, high-density development without addressing these foundational issues is not only unfair to existing residents—it also sets up future residents for hardship rather than success. In addition, the proposed RMF-45 zoning does not align with the existing character of our neighborhood. Approving this change would set a precedent for future high-density projects without adequate community engagement or long-term planning. Growth and housing solutions must be community-driven, thoughtfully integrated, and equitably distributed across Salt Lake City. I urge you to consider the cumulative impact of this zoning decision—not only on our neighborhood but on the individuals this project intends to serve. We all want a Salt Lake City that is inclusive and supportive, but that vision must be built through shared responsibility, balanced development, and planning that puts residents first. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Mackenzie Jaggi Salt Lake City Resident

comment: Councilman Puy: I hope all is well with you. I've appreciated your help in the past with the challenges and opportunities in our district in Salt Lake City. Today, I want to share feedback with you on some areas of concern that I understand will be addressed in an upcoming Council meeting. As you know, the planning commission approved an amendment put forward by the Mayor's office for a zoning change with more restrictions on parking in Salt Lake. This along with the "Road Diets", traffic calming, reduced street parking, higher fines and rates, and lower speed limits are choking the city. With these continued changes, it is becoming increasingly difficult to do business in Salt Lake City. With the city's multi-million dollar deficit, we should be looking for ways to increase business not raise taxes on a reduced amount of business. The restaurant tax is already at 8.75%. Other taxes have been implemented where Salt Lake City residents shouldn't an unfair share. The ongoing "road diets" add to commute times and I would suspect add to our pollution problem. Let's make Utah's Capitol City the best place to live, work, play AND do business. If we make it easier for people to do business in the City we will attract more businesses, more residents and more visitors. As a resident and business owner, I want only the best for Salt Lake City. Please do not support the Mayor's proposed zoning change. Thank you, Chris Hemmersmeier CEO Jerry Seine Dealerships

subject: SLC Public Safety Plan 2025 under performing__12

subject: Opportunity to protect Medicaid for homeless individuals
comment: Mayor and Council, As many of you know, my day job is state and federal health policy and I wanted to offer my support in the event you wanted to use your voice and connections to push back on proposed Medicaid cuts at the federal level. The clear connection is that cuts in funding or de facto cuts in funding through things like a work requirement would make it nearly impossible for individuals experiencing homelessness and getting behavioral health and/or drug use disorder treatment to maintain their coverage so they can exit the street-to-jail-to-street cycle. The easiest thing to do is to text our delegation and let them know this would hamper our efforts to promote safety in the city. I might also suggest reaching out to the donor class that have shown a particular interest on this topic (e.g. the Smith Entertainment Group, the LHM Group). Let me know if you want talking points or other resources. Happy to connect with anyone interested on this. Feel free to text me. -- Tom Merritt

comment: Ms. Petro-Eschler, The sign in the attached photo below was taken at the I-15 SB 3050 exit ramp to W 1300 S, SLC, UT 84115 Would it be possible to have a sign similar to the one below installed at: I-80 & Redwood Rd WB off ramp exit 118 I-215 & Redwood Rd WB off ramp exit 22 There continues to be panhandling at both off-ramps on a daily basis. subject: Thank you for you and your team's efforts on the Jordan River Trail on the West Side!
comment: Dear Chief Redd, I'm writing to extend my sincere thanks to you and your team for the increased enforcement efforts currently underway along the Jordan River Trail on the city's west side. These efforts have not gone unnoticed. For far too long, this beautiful stretch of our city has struggled under the weight of crime and unsafe conditions. The stepped-up patrols are making a real difference, and many of us who live near and use the trail regularly are finally beginning to feel a renewed sense of safety and pride in this public space. We are encouraged by the progress and deeply grateful for your department's commitment. It's our hope that this initiative will become a permanent presence to ensure the west side is no longer an afterthought when it comes to public safety. Our community deserves the same level of protection and peace of mind as every other part of Salt Lake City. Thank you again for your leadership and for prioritizing the wellbeing of all residents. Please extend our appreciation to the officers out on the trail each day—they're making a real impact. Warm regards, Ted Dumont Kevin Reeves

subject: homeless place to stay
comment: Respectfully, Council Members, I suggested a number of years ago (8 or 9) to the Mayor's office (and several times since) that what is needed is a "KOA" for those who do not want to be enclosed or who may be waiting for an opening in a shelter. I was originally told by the Mayor's office (each time) that it is not humane to leave them unsheltered (the official policy cannot be that the City expects them to remain unhoused). However, it is not "humane" to chase them from place to place as has been happening. I suggested the use of the old Fleet block but was told that it had contamination and could not be used. Now that it is demolished I hope it is actually being "de-contaminated". There is surely a block of land that can be fitted with lighting, water and hygiene facilities with trash removal and police oversight (just someone they can turn to for help if necessary - NOT guards as in a prison) that is more reasonable than expecting to build "tiny homes" and affordable housing. A regular place to stay with a small space for "stuff" which will also provide an address and prevent them from being CHASED all over the city. It will probably also be cheaper than spending weekly hazmat teams to clean up what is currently happening. Ellen Hardman

subject: Environmental Air Quality in the Lower Ave
comment: I have an environmental complaint about an all vegan barbecue restaurant that uses wood burning to cook its food. Two summers ago, at REDACTED, Blatch's Backyard BBQ started up its business in a house for sale in the historic section of Salt Lake City. Because of Utah's COVID-era regulations allowing home chefs to sell their food, this business received their permit without any input from nearby neighbors on what was being placed in the middle of a residential neighborhood. As in the past, when a resident wanted to add on to their house or make it taller, a notice on when and where the meeting would take place would be distributed around the neighborhood on those being affected. I have never seen such required paperwork. This business burn firewood and this results in the neighborhood filling up with varying degrees of smoke and soot in the air. This is especially harmful when we are close to inversion status. There is an apartment building next door to the business which in the summer when the residents turn on their air conditioners they bring that smoke and soot into their apartments. If we are concerned about air pollution in Salt Lake City, why isn't this business required at least to use propane instead of burning wood? If the lower avenue residents burned wood in there barbecue cookers instead of using propane, the air quality would be very unhealthy for sensitive groups including the elderly, asthmatics, diabetics, and heart and lung people. So I ask again, how did this business get the ok from the Salt Lake Business Community without going through proper procedures? If you don't live in this area then I suggest you take a walk between 5 and 7 on Wednesdays and Fridays and smell the air near this business. Also, notice the parking of cars near the business. It reminds me about how residents in the avenues used coal in their ovens long ago and filled the air with coal smoke. Sorry to be so verbose, but I'm trying to understand if we are concerned about air pollution and what we can do about it then why are we allowing a business to profit but yet make it harder on our health. Thank you for taking the time to view my point.

subject: Urgent Appeal for Unjust EV Charging Station Fines at Cottonwood Apartments and Alleged Political Discrimination
comment: Dear University of Utah Sustainability Office and Commuter Services, I am writing to vehemently appeal a series of $50 fines, accompanied by $3 per hour parking fees, recently imposed on my electric vehicle (EV) for not immediately removing it from a slow-charging station at the Cottonwood Apartments after it was fully charged. This policy is outrageously punitive, uniquely draconian, and a blatant betrayal of the university's sustainability commitments. It callously disregards the realities of EV users and, most disturbingly, appears to target me as a Tesla driver, possibly due to political biases against Elon Musk's policies and his association with Donald Trump. After a year of parking and charging at Cottonwood without a single fine, I am now slapped with daily $50 fines despite my consistent, lawful use. I demand an immediate reversal of these fines and a thorough investigation into what I suspect is vile political discrimination. For the past year, I have parked and charged my Tesla at Cottonwood Apartments without issue, always adhering to proper usage and parking protocols. Suddenly, I am now receiving daily $50 fines, a pattern that reeks of targeted harassment. I strongly suspect this is because I drive a Tesla, and the parking department is unfairly singling me out due to Elon Musk's political stances and his ties to Trump. This is not just an unjust policy—it is a disgusting display of political discrimination that has no place in an academic institution. Punishing me for my choice of vehicle is an affront to fairness and a shameful abuse of authority. The slow-charging stations take 10 to 12 hours to fully charge, depending on the battery level, making it utterly impossible to predict completion times accurately. Starting a charge at 8:00 PM, as I often do, could mean the vehicle finishes charging anytime from midnight to noon the next day. Demanding that users relocate their vehicle instantly—especially in the middle of the night when most are asleep—is absurd and deliberately cruel. This policy was clearly concocted by individuals who have never driven an EV and have zero regard for users' real-world constraints, such as the inability to act while sleeping or working. This policy is a shameful outlier. No other slow-charging stations in Salt Lake City, and virtually none nationwide, impose such an egregious combination of a $50 fine and hourly parking fees. This screams of arbitrary decision-making, devoid of research or consultation with EV users. The one-hour grace period is laughably inadequate for slow chargers, and the dual penalties are nothing short of predatory, especially when app notifications cannot guarantee immediate response due to users' commitments. Worse still, the charging stations at Cottonwood Apartments are never fully occupied. There are more than enough chargers, and even at peak times, many remain idle. This policy does not promote access—it actively discourages EV owners from charging, leaving stations desolate and unused. Rather than advancing the university's "U Drive Electric" program, which seeks to curb tailpipe emissions (nearly 50% of Utah's urban air pollution), this rule viciously penalizes environmentally conscious drivers like me and scares off prospective EV adopters, sabotaging the transition to sustainable energy. This policy is a direct assault on the University of Utah's sustainability commitments, including the "U Drive Electric" program and partnerships with Salt Lake City under the 2020 Electrified Transportation Resolution. It spits in the face of Salt Lake City's Climate Positive 2040 plan, which aims for 100% renewable electricity by 2030 and an 80% emissions reduction by 2040. By erecting barriers for EV users, the policy worsens air quality issues (vehicular emissions account for 40% of pollution) and mocks the university's goal of reducing transportation-related emissions (nearly 20% of campus emissions). I demand that you waive all recent $50 fines and urgently review this policy for the following reasons: 1. Unpredictable Charging Times: The 1-12 hour charging window makes immediate action impossible, especially overnight. 2. Unprecedented and Arbitrary Rule: No other slow-charging stations in Salt Lake City, and few nationwide, enforce such harsh penalties, exposing a lack of user-centric design. 3. Underutilized Chargers: Cottonwood's stations are never fully occupied, with ample availability, making the policy unnecessary and counterproductive as it deters charging entirely. 4. Lack of Empathy for EV Users: The policy ignores EV drivers' challenges, clearly crafted by those with no firsthand EV experience. 5. Suspected Political Discrimination: After a year of fine-free, lawful parking, daily $50 fines targeting my Tesla suggest bias against Musk's politics and Trump ties—a repugnant abuse of power. 6. Harm to Sustainability: The rule discourages EV use, hinders adoption, and undermines emissions reduction goals, betraying university and city objectives. As a dedicated EV owner, I am appalled by the university's failure to uphold its sustainability leadership. I value access to charging infrastructure, but policies must be just, rooted in EV users' realities, and aligned with environmental goals. This rule—singularly cruel, arbitrary, and disconnected from Cottonwood's underused chargers—achieves the opposite by discouraging charging, alienating eco-conscious drivers, and potentially discriminating based on political biases. I urge you to immediately reverse these fines, investigate any targeted harassment against Tesla drivers, and collaborate with EV users, Salt Lake City's Sustainability Department, and Utah Clean Energy to dismantle this disgraceful policy. Please contact me at REDACTED for further discussion. Thank you for your urgent attention to this matter.

subject: Disgraceful condition of SLC streets
comment: Dear SLC Council members, I am writing to complain about the terrible and disgraceful condition of many of the streets in Salt Lake City. Many of the streets in my neighborhood and all around the city are in incredibly bad condition and have been for years. Why has there not been regular and systematic maintenance to the surface streets in our city? I do not mean filling potholes. I mean resurfacing of streets that are full of cracks, old patched asphalt and big holes that get heavy traffic every day. I am an avid bicyclist and ride practically every day for commuting, shopping, pleasure and exercise April - November. Our streets are dangerous and unpleasant to ride on to say the least. This in no way encourages bicycling as an alternative to driving a car or for fitness. I sincerely invite any of you council members or the mayor to join me in a short ride around town to feel for yourselves the terrible condition of our streets. I have written to my council member for district #6, Dan Dugan, about this issue before and got a terse response to call the city streets department to report potholes. That is simply not a a satisfactory answer! Fix the d*** roads properly!! Municipal government's primary responsibility is to provide public safety and basic infrastructure. You are the leaders of our Salt Lake City government and you have let us down by not taking care of our streets. Please correct this long standing problem and prioritize the disgraceful disrepair of so many of our city streets. subject: Public Utilities budget and rate plan for 2025-26
comment: Last year I presented our HOA's concerns with the Public Utilities rate plan, in particular the new stabilization fees that treated our small HOA in an inequitable manner and had a severe impact on our finances. We were finally able to resolve the issue after several months of discussion with the City. Because we weren't aware of the new rate plan until after it went into effect in July 2025 we unfortunately had to pay the higher fees for several months until the issue was resolved. I'm hoping we can get ahead of our concern with another rate change for 2025-26 before it goes into effect. The new rate Public Utilities rate plan does make welcome changes for 2025-26, in particular by eliminating the stabilization fees and replacing them more focus on water usage, and by more equitably treating how water usage is charged across various customers. Using historical information about our HOA's water usage, we estimate that the new rate structure will save us approximately $500 per year on water usage. But the new sewer rate structure has changed to adversely effect multi-family organizations like our HOA (where one water meter serves a collection of homes) by using water usage year-round to compute sewer charges. We note that the PU's proposal allows single-family homes to use their average Winter water usage to compute sewer charges, but multi-family organizations like ours will use 70% of their ACTUAL water usage to compute sewer charges. Because we use significantly more water in non-Winter months for irrigation of our landscape, our water usage is up to 6 to 7 times higher in the Summer months. Using our historical water usage, this will equate to an estimated increase of $4500 per year in our sewer charges, or about $6000 more than what we would pay if we were charged using the new rate proposals for an equivalent number of single-family homes. Because all our irrigation water never ends up in the sewer, it seems highly inequitable for us to be charged a sewer fee for this water when single-family homes are not charged sewer fees for their irrigation water use. I will be presenting our concerns at the City Council meeting on May 20, but I'm hoping we can receive some feedback on this issue before then.

subject: Dismay with city ordinance 12.56.520 and its enforcement
comment: Hello, I am writing to express my dismay about a recent experience having my car towed in the Liberty Wells area because it was parked on the street too long under city ordinance 12.56.520. I have two complaints about this: One, I have to park on the street and it is unfeasible to expect me to move my car every two days; two, the cost of the tow was exorbitant and an undue financial burden. Where I live I do not have off-street parking, therefore I have to park on the street. I was on a trip and left my car parked on the street while I was gone. However, it was not in front of anyone's home and parked in an area rarely used by other cars (intentionally, to not take space where it is needed). There is plenty of off-street parking on my street (Westminster Ave). I feel that if anything there should be a residence permit for vehicles to park on the street without a time limit as I am sure there are many city residents in my situation, without off-street parking as an option. I do not drive much, therefore it is an unnecessary burden to have to get in my car every other day and move it up a spot to avoid violating city ordinance. I also feel that in general the parking limit of two days is much too short. My car was cited ($38 fee) and then promptly towed by CarTow. There was a warning left on the car two days before it was cited and towed, however as I was on a trip I did not see the warning. Luckily my partner noticed that the car was no longer on the street and discovered that it had been towed only two days after and was able to pick it up with a notarized email to avoid further storage costs. The cost of the tow and car storage fees were $360. Thus the whole ordeal cost around $400. My monthly rent is around $465, I am finishing grad school and therefore do not have a lot of income. $400 is almost my entire monthly rent payment and this cost feels like an exorbitant burden. I have had my car towed before in Washington DC for accidentally parking in a school loading area, and as I recall it was only around $130 including the parking citation. That financial burden feels much more reasonable. $400 is way too steep, I cannot believe the city council allows residents to be charged this much. I hope that you will consider two solutions to avoid this happening again in the future. One, city ordinance should be adjusted to allow for residence parking permits and a two-day limit is way too short, the limit should be significantly longer. Two, the city should not be allowing tow companies to charge so much. And why is the city piling a citation fee on top of the tow fee when the tow is already an undue financial burden ($360 in and of itself)? Sincerely, Casey Trout Resident of District 5

subject: Complaint for artificial turf - D2
comment: Good afternoon Alie, My name is Joseph Cowper. My family and I moved into your district last October at REDACTED. I want to start by informing you of the honor and respect I have for you taking a position of leadership for the city. I work in the financial services sector as a licensed Investment Specialist. As someone who is also in the "people" business, I can only imagine the nonsense you might experience as a government representative. I am reaching out to you to express frustration with a recent decision the council made regarding artificial turf. For context, earlier this week my family received a door-hanger from Angela Porter of Civil Enforcement citing that our home was in violation of the following codes: 21A.48.080B.4 21A.62.040 We had purchased the home with artificial turf on the parking strip and front yard. When we purchased the home, I can recall that it was disclosed to us that the city was not a fan of it on the parking strip. But I thought it was just that. I'll take accountability there and admit I should've looked into it further. Now I've taken some time to research this topic more. It seems that artificial turf has been banned in Salt Lake City since the 1990's and that decision was reinforced last year. We have since been told by civil enforcement that if we do not remove the turf by August or September of this year, we will be fined $25 per day. I'm not convinced the city will make an exception for our case so I've gone ahead and removed the turf. But my frustration lies in the negative experience we've endured and with the grounds the council has apparently made this decision on. As I understand it, the council believes that artificial turf is harmful to the environment. It contains a variety of damaging substances such as heavy metals, carcinogens, microplastics and/or more specifically SVOCs (semi-volatile organic compounds) and PFAs (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances). There's a concern that there are microplastics that run off into the water supply. It's argued that turf causes substantial heat to rise from the ground and into the air. Angela also informed me that it harms the organisms in the ground. I want to know how the council came to this decision. What studies has your team reviewed? From what I gather, the evidence used to make the claim 'artificial turf is harmful' is actually inconclusive. The city hasn't even offered to test my yard for the molecules of concern. You shouldn't make significant decisions like this on an unclear basis. As a result, I'm convinced the council is wrong and this decision is an overreach into my boundaries as a property owner. Furthermore, the ordinances still allow me to have artificial turf in my backyard. Some cities have the same ordinances as SLC but others don't. At a federal level, the evidence is still inconclusive. If artificial turf is truly as harmful to the environment as your team believes it to be, then you should strongly consider banning the material in all forms at all locations. Otherwise, the decision should be repealed. Utah faces significant water resource challenges and I feel that my artificial turf was an aesthetically pleasing way to do my part in being mindful of our elements. Additionally, the ordinances advise I must maintain 33% vegetation and less than 20% rocks within my front yard. How do you measure that? We didn't buy a home with a homeowner's association but it seems as though we're in one anyway. As you drive through my ZIP code you will notice that there are other homes in substantially worse condition. I know some of these people well and they have to work hard for what they already have. As a father of 2 young children, I get it, I don't want them to be subject to harmful substances or a polluted environment. I also keep an open mind. So if you think I'm wrong, I'd love for you to tell me why. I'm convinced we would agree on a lot but this event has caused me to have some big feelings. I'll level with you, I'd love to see my ZIP code become a more favorable place to live. I have a vision where our churches and charities have more resources to make significantly positive impacts. I'd love to see more businesses pop up. The homes in my area are over 100 years old, some that can really use some TLC. In fact, there are 3 projects that I'd love for us to talk more on: 1) Jordan River Trail; There are segments that are absolutely gross and the river is quite polluted with shopping carts and trash etc. 2) 864 Poplar Grove Blvd S; This is a vacant, falling apart home owned by the Salt Lake Redevelopment Agency. There's a real opportunity here to either rebuild or build a new home for a family that can use it. 3) Measurable and realistic solutions for homelessness; My closest grocery store is the Smith's at 828 S and 900 W. I call it the "hood pantry." But in all seriousness, the reality is that the entire intersection is a collecting ground for people in dire need. One of the homeless men I've talked to said he'd been in this situation for three years. Truthfully, it's not a comfortable area to be in. My hope is that you, not an assistant, thoughtfully read this email and thoughtfully respond. I wish you well and you are more than welcome to also give me a call. The Bible directs me to pray for our leadership and I want you to know that I do at the city, state, and federal level. Warm regards, Joseph Cowper

subject: Proposed water rate changes for fiscal year 2025/26
comment: Dear Salt Lake City elected officials, My name is Eric Kraan. I am a resident of Salt Lake County served by Salt Lake City Water. As a consequence, I feel less represented in the process of determining the changes taking to supply water when compared to a resident and constituent to whom you are accountable to. That said, those of us living outside of the city, are equally impacted by your choices and I ask that we are considered as equals through this process. I must say, who is accountable, who can we vote in or out, when we are satisfied or unsatisfied with the manner in which the problems of delivering this service does not meet our needs? (Attached to this email, you will find 2 water service bills I have paid. One for January 2023 and one for January 2025 that illustrate the doubling amount of basic rates within a 2-year period). I am PRIMARILY concerned about the rapidly increases to the basic cost of access to potable water. The lowest rate necessary for a household to maintain a basic level of sanitation has more than doubled in the past 2 years: JANUARY 2023: $26.68 JANUARY 2025: $57.03 Reviewing the proposed changes in the 2025/26 budget, it is clear that this cost is bound to continue to increase at a rate that far outpains the ability of those in fixed income or lower income households to meet the most basic level of sanitation, putting in danger the community's health and safety at large. It is for this reason that I this council must consider amending the proposed rate changes and make it a priority to maintain - perhaps even LOWER the basic cost of accessing water. This means reviewing the Fixed Charges (2 different charges) and Block 1 for its residential and multi-family customers. If additional revenue is needed to meet the regulatory expenses required on this service, these increases in revenue must be made through the commercial and higher blocks of water use which are not deemed essential for the safety, health and welfare of the community you represent (and even those you do not). If any of these fee increases are made to pay for increase capacity of the system to deliver water to the growing population expected within the SL Valley, it must be clearly delineated that future investment must be paid by the additional growth in subscribers to this service. Economic growth must be able to pay for itself, and not paid by putting current customers (especially those who can least afford to do so). That is, in essence, the true meaning of SUSTAINABLE GROWTH. I am confident that the members of this council and the Mayor's office will see the wisdom of engaging in truly progressive service fee increases. It must be a priority to maintain stability to the basic cost essential access to such a vital resource, and incrementally grow the system to accommodate the for population growth of our valley and bring about a more orderly, incremental, and sustainable pattern of development. These recent and proposed rate changes represent a chaotic pattern of growth that adds to the insecurity of vulnerable populations, decreases the trust of those who are concerned, and probably does not even register in the minds of those wealthy enough to keep lush green lawns, pools, and other luxury uses of water. Your attention to this important matter is greatly appreciated. Eric Kraan Resident of Cottonwood Heights.

subject: Inequitable Exceptions to Design Standards in Proposed MU Consolidation
comment: Ladies and Gentlemen of the City Council, We represent Madbrook Donut Company ("Madbrook"). Madbrook operates its bakery and main offices in a large building located at 375 West Hope Avenue in Salt Lake City. Currently Madbrook is zoned as CG. However, as part of the Planning Commission's proposed zoning changes (the "Proposal"), Madbrook's building will find itself in the MU-11 district. This is concerning because although a commercial bakery will continue to be an approved use, the building would potentially become a noncomptying structure under the proposed changes to Section 21A.37.050 of the Municipal Code. As this Proposal has proceeded, Madbrook has become increasingly concerned by the high burden that the new design standards will impose on many of the established buildings along the I-15 corridor. Further, it appears that there is very little, if any, exception or carve out for retailers, manufacturers, and other complying uses, but noncomptying structures unless the local business isn't really a local business, such as Walmart, Costco, and other bigger box retailers. Madbrook therefore remains concerned that the increased standards and minimal exceptions disproportionately affect smaller businesses like Madbrook. Specifically, when developing some of the newer Proposals, the Planning Commission Staff acknowledged "the reality that [certain] grocery stores generally do not meet the regulations and will not unless completely redeveloped," and therefore made sure that "the MU-3 specifically includes a waiver of the Design Review threshold and Design Standards compliance to allow for some by-right additions to such large commercial noncomptying structures." September 25, 2024 Staff Report at 9. The Staff thus proposed "additions allowance[s]" whereby a grocery store over 10,000 square feet be allowed expansions of a maximum footprint of 7,500 square feet (a 75% expansion) without the requirement of undergoing Design Review or complying with the Design Standards. Although the numbers have changed slightly, the accommodation persists for businesses lucky enough to find themselves in the MU-3 zone, but not those who land in the MU-11 zone. As a result, if the Proposal is passed as currently submitted, Madbrook and many other businesses along the I-15 corridor will not enjoy the same sort of additions allowance despite also inhabiting a reality where their buildings "do not meet the regulations and will not unless completely redeveloped" -- just like those in the MU-3 zone. Instead, these businesses are left wondering how much of an addition or change to their structures would trigger the necessity of remodeling the entire building to fit the Design Standards. Madbrook asks that if the City Council and Planning Commission are considering the undue burden on already established buildings in the MU-3 zone, it do so uniformly and codify the same type of exceptions in the MU-11 zone. The Proposal also discusses the creation of a Transitional Overlay over the zone in which Madbrook's building is located. See id. § 21A.34.030. Buildings in this Overlay may access relaxed design standards if either (1) they implement a series of several landscaping measures or (2) they are a pre-existing "large" retailer with more than 100,000 square feet of floor space. This limited exception that ignores buildings in the I-15 corridor means that businesses that have approved and conforming uses might incur significant demolition and remodeling even under the relaxed standards. However, the largest retailers, such as Walmart – which is across the street from Madbrook and within spitting distance, The Home Depot, and Costco all receive immediate access the relaxed standards just by virtue of their size. In essence, the City would be prioritizing protecting the largest retailers (and not local businesses) from the new requirements – even though those retailers arguably have more resources and capital to do so. This may mean that smaller businesses will have no choice but to move or go out of business, just allowing more lucrative and bigger boxes to fill the void. This is simply unfair. The Proposal's effort to create addition allowances and relaxed standards for some of the businesses that are most affected by the changes is admirable, but in its current state, it creates inequity by hand-selecting only a few favored businesses, in certain parts of the new zones, to benefit from the changes while ignoring similarly-situated businesses that even have approved uses. While there are many walkable areas in Salt Lake City that may benefit from these design standards, applying them to the I-15 corridor that has historically contained industrial and manufacturing uses now, without making exceptions, is unfair and robs these owners of their expected return on their investments – both in their real estate and their businesses. Accordingly, we respectfully request that the City Council deny the Proposal in its current state with directions to the Planning Commission to create more equitable exceptions that allow for the same addition allowances and/or the same relative relaxation of standards via the Transitional Overlay for all businesses with an approved use, but potentially a nonconforming structure. Thank you for your time and consideration. Best regards, Adam D. Goff BENNETT TUELLER JOHNSON & DEERE

subject: Mixed Use Zoning Consolidation Comments
comment: Council Chair and Members of the Salt Lake City Council, Thank you for the opportunity to speak today regarding the proposed Mixed use zoning consolidation. My name is Amy Stocks, and I am the owner of the property at REDACTED. I'm speaking not only as a homeowner, but as someone deeply invested in the future of Salt Lake City's neighborhoods and in the issue of housing stability. The proposed zone change from TSA to MU 5 will directly impact the lot immediately south of my 1958 single-story home on its humble 25' wide lot. I understand the city's interest in simplifying zoning and easing the administrative burden—but doing so at the expense of long-term residents and the character of our neighborhoods is not responsible governance. It prioritizes developer convenience over community wellbeing. That tradeoff is not just unacceptable—it's short-sighted. This zoning change would allow buildings up to 55-65 feet tall with drastically reduced setbacks—shrinking the buffer between my property and a potential six-story structure from over 60 feet under current zoning to just 20 feet. That would overwhelm my home, eliminate privacy, block sunlight, and prevent me from growing a garden, installing solar panels, or enjoying my backyard—fundamentally changing how I live in my own home. - I am not aware of the example of the effects of this consolidation. This is not how we create thriving, livable communities. It is a one-size-fits-all approach that disregards context, ignores history, and weakens the social and architectural fabric of Salt Lake's diverse neighborhoods. Fairpark is not Ballpark, and Fleet Block is not Maven State. Yet this rezone treats every area as interchangeable. Worse, the developers pushing this change have not earned the community's trust. In Fairpark, they have misrepresented property sales, allowed purchased homes to fall into disrepair, and contributed to visible blight—vacant houses, overgrown lots, and increased trash. They offer long-time residents below-market prices and then rent them with no upkeep while waiting for this rezone to pass. This is speculative development at its most predatory. And while the city justifies this rezone in part on the need for affordable housing, what's being proposed doesn't meet that need. Studio apartments at 60% AMI are not truly affordable for families or many individuals in Fairpark and surrounding neighborhoods. Let me be clear: I support smart, inclusive growth. But growth must be done with intention. Each neighborhood has different needs, different histories, and different capacities for change. This blanket rezone flattens those differences and gives developers a free pass to build quickly, cheaply, and without accountability to the people who already live here. Salt Lake City has a chance to do better. We can create policies that encourage density and creativity, affordability and livability. That starts by revising this zoning amendment—especially its regulations on height, setbacks, active frontage, and parking—to reflect the values of our communities and the reality on the ground. We don't need another corridor of cookie-cutter buildings. We need neighborhoods we can be proud of—places where history, culture, and community aren't sacrificed for short-term profit. Salt Lake City is better than this. And I believe you are too. Thank you. Amy Stocks

subject: Mu zoning consolidation zoning text and map amendment
comment: Please read. While high-density housing developments are frequently touted as solutions to urban sprawl and housing shortages, they also present substantial social, environmental, and infrastructural challenges that warrant meticulous reevaluation. Infrastructure and Service Strain High-density housing concentrates large populations into confined geographical areas, exerting immense strain on existing infrastructure such as roads, sewage systems, public transportation, and utilities. Many cities lack the requisite resources or foresight to upgrade these systems at the requisite pace. Consequently, residents may encounter increased traffic congestion, overburdened public transportation, water shortages, and degraded public services—all of which diminish the quality of life. Community and Livability Erosion Dense housing developments, particularly large apartment complexes and high-rise buildings, can undermine community cohesion. Detached single-family neighborhoods often foster stronger social bonds, as individuals have more space to congregate, interact, and engage with their neighbors. Conversely, high-density living can engender anonymity, social isolation, and diminished civic engagement. Furthermore, overcrowding can exacerbate noise pollution, restrict access to green spaces, and diminish personal privacy. Environmental Concerns While proponents contend that high-density housing diminishes urban sprawl and car dependency, the environmental advantages are not always unequivocal. Tall buildings necessitate substantial energy for construction and maintenance (particularly heating, cooling, and vertical transportation). Additionally, higher population densities can lead to localized air pollution hotspots, diminished biodiversity, and heat island effects, which adversely impact urban microclimates. Public Health Risks High-density living environments have been demonstrated to facilitate the rapid spread of infectious diseases, as evidenced by the COVID-19 pandemic. Close proximity, shared ventilation systems, and common spaces hinder the effective control of outbreaks. Mental health can also be adversely affected, as studies have associated crowded living conditions with elevated rates of anxiety, depression, and stress. Aesthetic and Cultural Impact Dense housing developments frequently conflict with the architectural heritage and character of established neighborhoods. Large, uniform apartment complexes can diminish cultural identity, diminish historical value, and create monotonous urban landscapes that many individuals find unappealing. These developments pose a risk of replacing vibrant and diverse neighborhoods with bland and impersonal environments. Bill

subject: Zoning Consolidation
comment: For the sake of our city's future, we need to simplify, streamline, and liberalize our zoning. Most of the issues our city faces are downstream of the decades-long failure to build housing. Yes, we've been building a lot of new apartment buildings, but the complex zoning and approval processes means that these are the only sort of buildings that can be put up profitably. Streamlining zoning would enable both a larger volume of housing to be built, but a larger variety, too. There are many empty and abandoned properties across the city that could have housing built on it. More housing of all types is essential, and we must allow people to build more housing if they see people sit on their own properties, too. Please simplify the city's zoning and approval process.

subject: Trash Fees
comment: Hi, Like many of our fees trash fees are both too high and too low. The customers of Salt Lake City's Sustainability Department should be given more control over their trash fees by charging on a size of can and per pickup basis...this will also better reflect the size of demand a given household places on the system. For instance: my household produces about 1 40 gallon trashcan of trash per month and 1 recycle bin per month and then composts much of our organic waste on site. Yet, we pay the same as my neighbor who overfills their 90 gallon can every week. I essentially subsidize their pickup by being frugal with the amount of trash we produce. We should make the cost of a 40 gallon can proportional to a 90...i.e a 40 gallon can costs $8/pickup and a 90 gallon costs $18/pickup and only charge per pickup. This will result in the highest income houses (those with the largest amounts of trash, typically) paying the most and will encourage houses to recycle and compost. It will also help houses downsize their cans. This should also decrease in-city pollution by decreasing the number of stops and starts of our trash service. Blake Quinton

subject: Community Concerns: Proposed Rezoning in Rio Grande District
comment: Dear City Council Members, I am a resident of the Rio Grande neighborhood and am writing to express my concerns regarding the proposed rezoning to allow high-rise development in our district. I believe this change could significantly alter the human scale and character that make our community unique. I respectfully request that you: 1. Pause any rezoning or up-zoning actions for this area until a comprehensive infrastructure capacity study (roads, water, sewer, schools) is completed and published. 2. Maintain current height limits and density restrictions, ensuring new projects remain in scale with existing buildings. 3. Require a full Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) under NEPA and State law before proceeding, so residents can review detailed analyses of traffic, air quality, water runoff, and historic preservation impacts. 4. Hold a dedicated public hearing focused solely on the Rio Grande District plan, with sufficient notice and outreach to ensure all affected residents can be heard. I plan to submit these same comments in writing at the City Council meeting on May 20, 2025 (6 p.m., City & County Building) and at the Redevelopment Advisory Committee meeting on June 4, 2025 (4 p.m., 451 S. State St., Room 126). I hope you will stand with your constituents to safeguard the human-scaled character that makes our neighborhood special. Thank you for your time and consideration. subject: Granary Parking Garage
comment: Dear Mayor, Mendenhall, and City Council, As the Granary District Alliance, GDA, we're contacting you directly due to growing concern of the parking garage in our district, located at 500 W. and 700 S. The Granary District is growing and thriving faster than ever. This summer, businesses in our district plan to bring over 250,000 people to the Granary district between now and November. We also know that when big events are happening, smaller businesses struggle to have parking spots available to their customers, forcing them to walk many blocks. We've noticed reductions in street parking along 500 S., on 400 W., and as business owners, we are collectively concerned about not having the parking garage available to assist with parking demands. It is too often we see drivers not adhering to speed limits (500 W.), ignoring/not seeing stop signs (400 W. and 700 S.), and creating traffic jams (700 S.) while trying to find parking. We are formally requesting expedited attention to getting the parking garage open as soon as possible, preferably sometime early this summer. We know the city is working closely with the owners to get permits in motion and the garage open, but with the parking garage nearly one year behind schedule, we feel we need extra focus put on this big puzzle piece to solving parking limitations in our district. Last summer and fall, due to high attendance events in our area, we noticed many attendees parking on city streets, not following street signs, parking or blocking bike lanes, or walking down the street because there was no sidewalk space. This all puts the public in danger, especially since a majority of our entertainment events like Granary Live, brewery events, Fear Factory Haunted House, etc., happen in the evening with limited light. Please join us in doing everything you can to ensure the Granary district is a thriving and positive experience for everyone. We need a place for our customers, staff and residents to park safely and are asking for your help in expediting this process at the parking garage located at 500 W. And 700 S. Sincerely, The Granary District Alliance Board A formal copy of this message in letter format is attached.

On a recent cold and weather threatening morning, in one hour, I collected 30 signatures supporting the construction of new trails. I have attached the list. This is not a formal petition, just an indication that the much ballyhooed and then terminated trail construction has popular support (and twice received approval from the commissioned study partners). Full disclosure: one person refused to sign saying that we have enough trails. That translates to 97% in favor of SLC joining all the communities in Utah embracing trails as a means of drawing visitors and allowing residents to enjoy the natural beauty of Utah It is ironic that SOF makes (or in the past has made) the conflicting claims that we do not need more trails and that user conflict is out of hand. Salt Lake County has the largest number of High School mountain bike team members of any county in the whole country. If the City and County want to retain these citizens as they enter the workforce it is important to give them recreational as well as economic reasons to stay. These team members do more for trail maintenance than any other user group so all users should be grateful the teams exist. A constant problem in SLC is air pollution. Building a trail system in the foothills above the city will reduce pollution as fewer people will be forced to drive to Draper and Herriman to enjoy trails. Thank you for your attention. subject: Sunnyside Park Go Bond proposals.
comment: City Leaders, My baseball program is experiencing unprecedented growth, and I'm actively working to expand opportunities for young athletes throughout the city. We don't just need to maintain our current field capacity – we need more fields to accommodate this growth. This season I grew my program by more than 75 participants to 365 kids. By 2027, I fully expect to have over 500 kids in my program alone. If that growth pattern continues across all east side youth baseball leagues, we'll have approximately 1,000 participants needing field space in the coming years. With the arrival of the MLB in our city I can only expect those numbers to continue to rise. I currently rent two Dilworth elementary baseball fields, and I found out recently Highland High school will be renovating one of those fields for their High School Baseball program while theirs is being used for the rebuild of Highland high school. basically, removing that field and probably the other field also from my available rental spaces. This makes this Sunnyside situation even more critical as I'm already losing a field, so I need to make up for that field somewhere and we don't have any fields on the east side to make it up! Another challenge is I have heard that there are fields on the west side however no parent on the east side wants to travel to the west side of our city to play or practice baseball. So west side baseball fields and complexes are simply not an option for families on the east side who race home from work to get their kids to a practice 15 - 20 minutes away from their homes. That is an unreasonable expectation for recreational baseball participants and coaches etc. A crucial part of our growth plan includes creating a Babe Ruth division, which requires a full-size field with 90 bases and 300' fences. I'm not seeing this type of field in any of the current proposals, despite having requested it during earlier input phases. This is a significant oversight that will limit opportunities for our older players. That field can be used for younger divisions also. Currently, before the Utah baseball stadium project, Sunnyside Park had five softball/baseball fields that could have provided vital space for our activities. I understand that softball fields can serve as excellent mixed-use facilities - we can utilize them for baseball when they're not being used by softball leagues. However, with the west field already being lost to the University of Utah stadium development and additional fields potentially being removed in proposals B and C, we're moving in exactly the wrong direction. The only proposal I can remotely support is Proposal A, as it removes the fewest fields. However, even this option falls short of what our community truly needs - more baseball facilities, not fewer. Proposals B and C would be devastating to youth baseball in this area, effectively eliminating three fields from the available pool (one taken by the stadium and two completely removed from the park). Youth sports must be the priority in our city planning. Once baseball fields are removed, we will never get them back. The east side already lacks adequate facilities compared to the demand we're seeing, and reducing field capacity further would force us to turn away children who want to play. I strongly urge you to reconsider all current proposals with an eye toward increasing, not decreasing, the number of fields available for youth sports. At minimum, we need to preserve every possible existing field, and ideally, we should be looking for opportunities to add facilities, including a regulation-size Babe Ruth field. If we can keep even the one softball field, I can rent that for the Babe Ruth age kids ages 13-16. I believe there's an opportunity here to create a park that truly serves the exploding interest in youth baseball on the east side. Thank you for considering these urgent concerns. Sincerely, August Wachter President Foothill Youth Baseball Association

subject: City Council Comment: Fox Squirrels
comment: Hello, I would like to ask the City Council to consider doing something about the rapidly increasing population of fox squirrels in Salt Lake City. These squirrels are becoming more numerous every year and pose a serious threat to many of the trees in Salt Lake. They are an invasive species and have driven out our native red squirrels. They harm trees by chewing off sections of leaves and peeling bark off that in some cases can kill a tree. In the past, the electric company had a squirrel abatement program to keep squirrels form chewing through wires. As they increased the thickness of their wires, they no longer had a problem with squirrels and discontinued that program. We are now greatly in need of a similar program to protect the city's trees (as well as internet wires — I and others I know have had outages created by fox squirrels). I hope the City Council will consider doing something about these squirrels as an already bad situation becomes even worse with the rapid increase in their population. Thank you for your consideration. Sincerely, Steve Roens

(Hillside Middle School, Coygrill Elementary, Beacon Heights Elementary, and Foothill Montessori of Salt Lake). There have been an increasing number of safety concerns brought up with the street and to the Mayor's office, the School District, and school Principles through the years. That said, people like myself are sharing more than our share of the burden. I am a widowed senior, living alone with a very modest lifestyle. I subscribe to the smallest available garbage container (40 gallons) that I have collected once EVERY 6-8 WEEKS (and it is never full); my recycling bin is put out never more than 1x/month; I compost nearly all my kitchen and yard waste so the "brown bin" is only used in the fall when I collect leaves from the street (the city's responsibility, but you're a bit slow) that I don't want to put on my vegetable gardens. Modern technology should easily allow you to know how often (and how much) my waste is collected. Can't I be billed accordingly? The only incentive we have to contribute less waste to the system is the tiered rate of the garbage containers and that rate favors the largest users-- they get 2.25 more capacity for 0.5 more cost.
